lead: Every CMOS chip needs both an NMOS and a PMOS. An NMOS needs a p-type body; a PMOS needs an n-type body. One silicon substrate can supply only one doping, so the other device must sit in a locally doped well. The p-well, n-well and twin-tub processes are three answers to the same question: which device goes inside a well, and how freely can each body be doped? The choice fixes mask count, body resistance, threshold voltages and latch-up behaviour, and it appears in every CMOS process flow.
prereq: You need: the chapter on nMOS and CMOS fabrication process flow and the topic Threshold voltage and body effect.

sections.h3: Why one device must sit in a well

blocks.text: An NMOS conducts when electrons are pulled through a p-type body toward an n+ drain. A PMOS conducts when holes are pulled through an n-type body toward a p+ drain. The body is the terminal that sets the channel type and the threshold voltage. A plain silicon wafer is doped either p-type or n-type throughout; it cannot be both at the surface. The well solves this. A well is a deep doped region formed early in the flow, before the gate stack, by ion implantation and a high-temperature drive. The device inside the well uses the well as its body. The device outside uses the substrate as its body.

The well-substrate junction must stay reverse biased. An n-well sits in a p-substrate and is tied to the most positive supply. A p-well sits in an n-substrate and is tied to the most negative supply. The well is deep, not a thin sheet, so its doping and size affect junction capacitance and the parasitic devices discussed in the chapter on latch-up in CMOS and its prevention.

In a p-well process the wafer starts n-type. A p-well holds the NMOS; the PMOS sits in the n-substrate. The n-substrate is tied to VDD. In an n-well process the wafer starts p-type. An n-well holds the PMOS; the NMOS sits in the p-substrate, which is tied to VSS. This is the common choice. The NMOS keeps the lightly doped substrate as its body. In a twin-tub process the starting wafer is usually p-type, but both an n-well and a p-well are implanted and driven separately. The PMOS body is the n-well; the NMOS body is the p-well. Each well has its own doping dose, so both threshold voltages and both body-effect coefficients can be set. The price is one extra well mask and a longer thermal budget.

blocks.text: Most digital CMOS uses n-well. The NMOS, which carries most of the logic current, sits in the lightly doped substrate, where its electron mobility is high and its junction capacitance and body effect are low; the well dose is then chosen to suit the PMOS. A p-type wafer at VSS suits the whole die, and the flow grew straight out of the older nMOS process. For latch-up, the wafer is often a thin, lightly doped p-epitaxial layer on a heavily doped p+ substrate, whose low resistance shunts the parasitic path. Twin-tub costs one mask but gives independent control; it appears in low-voltage, analog and mixed-signal processes where matching and body effect matter. A triple-well process adds a deep n-well under a p-well. That isolates the p-well from the p-substrate, so a block of NMOS can have its own body bias, or a noisy digital block can be separated from analog devices. Silicon-on-insulator goes further: a buried oxide layer isolates the transistor body from the wafer, removing the well-substrate junction. SOI gives lower capacitance and no latch-up path, but the wafer is more expensive; only a few universities teach it in detail. The parasitic bipolar path itself is left to the chapter on latch-up in CMOS and its prevention.

examples.question: A twin-tub process lets the designer choose the NMOS body doping. Compare an NMOS built straight in a lightly doped p-substrate (N<sub>A</sub> = 1×10¹⁵ cm⁻³) with one built in a p-well (N<sub>A</sub> = 1×10¹⁷ cm⁻³). Both have t<sub>ox</sub> = 10 nm, so C<sub>ox</sub> = 3.45×10⁻⁷ F/cm². Take ε<sub>Si</sub> = 1.04×10⁻¹² F/cm, q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, n<sub>i</sub> = 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ and kT/q = 0.0259 V. (a) Find the body-effect coefficient γ = √(2qε<sub>Si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>)/C<sub>ox</sub> for each. (b) Find the threshold rise ΔV<sub>T</sub> = γ(√(2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub>) − √(2φ<sub>F</sub>)) at V<sub>SB</sub> = 1 V, with φ<sub>F</sub> = (kT/q)·ln(N<sub>A</sub>/n<sub>i</sub>).
steps: Substrate, N<sub>A</sub> = 1×10¹⁵: 2qε<sub>Si</sub>N<sub>A</sub> = 2 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × 1.04×10⁻¹² × 10¹⁵ = 3.31×10⁻¹⁶; the square root is 1.82×10⁻⁸.
p-well, N<sub>A</sub> = 1×10¹⁷: the doping is 100 times larger, so γ is √100 = 10 times larger: γ = 0.53 V<sup>½</sup>.
φ<sub>F</sub>: substrate 0.0259 × ln(10⁵) = 0.298 V, so 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.596 V; p-well 0.0259 × ln(10⁷) = 0.417 V, so 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.835 V.
examples.answer: γ = 0.053 V<sup>½</sup> in the substrate and 0.53 V<sup>½</sup> in the p-well; at V<sub>SB</sub> = 1 V the threshold rises by 0.026 V and 0.23 V. The heavier well gives about nine times the body effect, which is why a twin-tub process sets each well dose on purpose.

examples.question: In an n-well process μn = 500 cm²/V·s and μp = 200 cm²/V·s. (a) For a symmetric inverter, find Wp/Wn. (b) With L = 0.5 μm and Wn = 2 μm, find Wp. (c) Which transistor sits inside the well, and which carrier sets the speed?
steps: A symmetric inverter has equal pull-up and pull-down current at the same supply. Set μn(W/L)n = μp(W/L)p.
The channel length L is the same for both devices, so it cancels. Wp/Wn = μn/μp = 500/200 = 2.5.
The given L = 0.5 μm is not needed for the ratio or for Wp because it cancels in the current balance.
The PMOS sits in the n-well. Electrons in the NMOS have higher mobility than holes in the PMOS, so the NMOS sets the speed and the PMOS must be wider.
examples.answer: Wp/Wn = 2.5, Wp = 5 μm; the PMOS sits in the n-well and electrons in the NMOS set the speed.
examples.check:
mun = 500
mup = 200
ratio = mun / mup
Wn = 2
Wp = ratio * Wn
print(ratio)
print(Wp)

traps: Saying the n-well process puts the NMOS in a well. It does not: the NMOS stays in the p-substrate and only the PMOS is in the n-well.
Swapping the bodies: in a p-well process the NMOS is in the p-well and the PMOS is in the n-substrate.
Thinking twin-tub is just two names for one well. It uses two independently doped wells and one extra well mask, so both Vt and body effect can be set.
Using the mobility ratio upside down. Holes are slower, so Wp/Wn = μn/μp is greater than one.
Believing the well is a thin surface layer. It is a deep region whose doping and depth affect parasitic capacitance and latch-up.

quiz.q: Which device sits inside the n-well in an n-well CMOS process?
quiz.a: The PMOS sits inside the n-well; the NMOS sits in the p-substrate.

quiz.q: Why must one transistor sit in a well?
quiz.a: An NMOS needs a p-type body and a PMOS needs an n-type body. One substrate has only one doping, so the other body must be a local well.

quiz.q: A process has μn = 600 cm²/V·s and μp = 240 cm²/V·s. Find Wp/Wn for a symmetric inverter.
Why do most digital processes choose n-well rather than p-well?
quiz.a: The NMOS, which does most of the logic work, stays in the lightly doped p-substrate, so its mobility stays high and its body effect and junction capacitance stay low; only the PMOS pays for the heavier well doping. The p-substrate at VSS suits the whole die, and a p-epi on p<sup>+</sup> wafer adds a low-resistance substrate against latch-up.

quiz.q: How many independent well dopings does a twin-tub process have?
quiz.a: Two: one n-well doping and one p-well doping, each set separately.

quiz.q: What does twin-tub buy in exchange for one extra mask?
quiz.a: Independent doping of the NMOS p-well and the PMOS n-well, so both threshold voltages and both body-effect coefficients can be set.

quiz.q: Give one use of a triple-well process.
quiz.a: A deep n-well isolates a p-well from the p-substrate, so an NMOS block can have its own body bias or be separated from noisy digital devices.

quiz.q: The p-well NMOS of the worked example (γ = 0.53 V<sup>½</sup>, 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.835 V) has its source 2 V above its body. Find ΔV<sub>T</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production CMOS moved from twin-tub to triple-well and then to FinFET and FD-SOI for body isolation and low leakage. Search 'twin-tub CMOS process', 'triple-well latch-up' and 'FD-SOI body bias' for process detail.
